title: Fennel
subtitle: The carminative seed: infusions and compresses for colic, wind, and cramps
excerpt: Fennel seed is the most widely available carminative herb in most kitchen spice cupboards. The dried seeds are brewed as a simple hot infusion for wind, bloating, and digestive spasm. The same infusion, cooled, makes an eye compress for tired or inflamed eyes. A jar of dried fennel seeds keeps two years in a sealed tin.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931), fennel entry, Botanical.com transcription. Nicholas Culpeper, Complete Herbal (1653), fennel entry, public domain. EMA HMPC Community herbal monograph on Foeniculum vulgare Miller subsp. vulgare var. vulgare, fructus (2007, EMA/HMPC/137845/2006), open access.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb or preparation that relieves wind and digestive bloating by relaxing smooth muscle in the gut wall and allowing trapped gas to disperse.

content.text: Fennel seed in the home medicine cupboard, gently crushed dried seeds brewed as a hot infusion for wind, bloating, and intestinal cramp. The most kitchen-friendly

herb, already in most spice cupboards, with a long use in European and Ayurvedic cooking and home medicine for digestive discomfort after meals. A jar of dried seeds keeps two years, and a fresh batch of seeds from a fennel plant in the garden is easily dried and stored.

attrs.title: Precautions
attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Foeniculum vulgare Mill., family Apiaceae. A tall aromatic perennial or biennial, up to 2 m, with blue-green feathery leaves, flat-topped yellow flower heads, and small oblong seeds (technically fruits) in pairs. Native to the Mediterranean. naturalised across coastal and disturbed ground in temperate regions worldwide. The seeds, gathered when ripe in late summer and dried, are the part used in digestive preparations. The root, leaf, and stem are edible vegetables in their own right.

The seed carries a volatile oil rich in trans-anethole (50 to 80%), fenchone, and estragole. fixed oils. flavonoids. and coumarins. The wind-easing action comes from the volatile oil relaxing smooth muscle in the gut wall, allowing trapped gas to move. Anethole is also a plant oestrogen, hence the use for promoting milk flow and the cautions for oestrogen-sensitive conditions. The current European herbal guidance reference entry supports traditional use of bitter fennel seed for mild digestive complaints including meteorism and spasmodic gastrointestinal complaints.

The 17th-century herbalist Culpeper recommended fennel seed for urinary complaints and for wind in the stomach. The 20th-century herbalist Grieve covers fennel water for infant colic, fennel tea for gas, and its use as a digestive spice. The Ayurvedic tradition uses fennel as a digestive after meals and to support milk flow in nursing mothers. Current herbal guidance supports traditional use for digestive complaints, gas, and mild spasm.

Hot infusion: 1 teaspoon of crushed fennel seeds per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 10 minutes. Crush the seeds lightly in a mortar before brewing to help release the volatile oil. Strain and drink after meals, up to three cups a day.

Eye compress: brew a double-strength infusion (2 teaspoons per 200 ml), cool completely, strain carefully through muslin. Soak two cotton pads in the cooled liquid and lay over closed eyes for 5 to 10 minutes. A traditional use for tired or mildly irritated eyes. not a substitute for medical assessment of eye symptoms.
Pregnancy: culinary fennel is safe. Avoid regular medicinal doses in pregnancy, especially in the first three months. Consult a herbalist or midwife.

Oestrogen-sensitive conditions: take care. Fennel contains plant oestrogens. If you have or have had an oestrogen-sensitive cancer, or take hormone therapy, speak to your specialist before taking medicinal fennel.
